claims.text: The relevant FeMnNiGeSi-type alloy has an ordered, single-phase hexagonal initial state.
The initial alloy exhibits a sharp first-order magnetostructural transition.
The initial alloy has large magnetization or transition hysteresis.
Bulk arc-melted ingots and melt-spun microribbons have limited heat-exchange area.
Changing substrate temperature during sputter deposition changes the density of grain boundaries, twin interfaces, and defect clusters in FeMnNiGeSi films.
Nano-scale heterogeneities induce local strain fields in the alloy.
Nano-scale defects act as localized nucleation sites for the magnetostructural transition.
Defect-induced strain and nucleation modify the abrupt first-order transition into a more gradual transition.
Broadening the magnetostructural transition reduces hysteretic losses.
Increasing nano-scale defect density increases effective surface area and improves heat exchange.
Lower substrate temperatures yield higher defect densities than higher substrate temperatures.
Lower-temperature-deposited films will exhibit a broader magnetization transition than the baseline bulk forms.
Lower-temperature-deposited films will exhibit a smaller hysteresis width than the baseline bulk forms.
Lower-temperature-deposited films may exhibit a multi-stage magnetostructural transition.
Lower-temperature-deposited films will have greater surface roughness and effective area than the baseline bulk forms.
Greater film surface roughness and area will improve heat exchange during low-field magnetic cycling.
The qualitative relationship between nano-scale heterogeneity and reduced hysteresis is supported by analogous material systems.

contradictions.description: The requested and proposed intervention concerns as-deposited sputtered thin films, but the stated initial state and baseline are arc-melted ingots or melt-spun microribbons. Arc melting is not a deposition process, and comparing low-temperature films with bulk forms confounds substrate temperature with fabrication route and sample geometry.

The hypothesis attributes improved heat exchange partly to defect-controlled surface area, whereas the prediction compares thin films with bulk forms. The thin-film form factor itself changes surface-to-volume ratio, so this comparison does not isolate the claimed defect-mediated effect.

The falsification rule requires both no change in heterogeneity and no change in transition behavior. Failure of substrate temperature to change the proposed mediator shows an ineffective intervention rather than falsifying the mediator mechanism; conversely, a measured heterogeneity change without the predicted hysteresis response would directly challenge the mechanism but is not declared falsifying.
